intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PAK2 gene.

checks.claim: Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PAK2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We conclude that the KNO2 syndrome in the studied family is dominant and caused by a deleterious variant in the PAK2 gene.
checks.explanation: The abstract calls the variant monoallelic, which means the same as heterozygous.

paragraphs.text: Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is a disorder characterized by retinal degeneration and encephalocele, together with intellectual disability and autistic behavior, that is not linked to the COL18A1 locus. In the single reported family it showed dominant transmission and was caused by a heterozygous variant in the PAK2 gene (Antonarakis et al., 2021).

checks.claim: Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is characterized by retinal degeneration and encephalocele.
checks.evidence_quote: KNO2 (Knobloch type 2 syndrome with intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, encephalocele)
checks.explanation: Retinal degeneration and encephalocele are both named among the KNO2 features.

checks.claim: Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is characterized by intellectual disability and autistic behavior.
checks.evidence_quote: KNO2 (Knobloch type 2 syndrome with intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, encephalocele)
checks.explanation: Intellectual disability and autistic behavior are both named among the KNO2 features.

checks.claim: Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is not linked to the COL18A1 locus.
checks.evidence_quote: Linkage to the COL18A1 locus was excluded in the New Zealand family, providing evidence for the existence of a second KNO locus. We named the second unmapped locus for Knobloch syndrome KNO2.
checks.explanation: The paper defines KNO2 as the locus in a family where linkage to COL18A1 was excluded.

checks.claim: In the single reported family with KNO2, the disorder showed dominant transmission.
checks.evidence_quote: We conclude that the KNO2 syndrome in the studied family is dominant
checks.explanation: The paper concludes dominance in the family it studied. The abstract does not say this is the only reported family.

checks.claim: In the single reported family with KNO2, the disorder was caused by a heterozygous variant in the PAK2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The variant was monoallelic and apparently de novo in both siblings
checks.explanation: The monoallelic causative PAK2 variant is supported. The abstract does not say this is the only reported family.

paragraphs.text: Menzel et al. (2004) named the second, then unmapped, locus for Knobloch syndrome KNO2.

checks.claim: Menzel et al. (2004) named the second, then unmapped, locus for Knobloch syndrome KNO2.
checks.evidence_quote: We named the second unmapped locus for Knobloch syndrome KNO2.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: Wilson et al. (1998) reported 2 sibs with high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration, and occipital encephalocele or scalp lesion. One sib had very early onset of severe eye disease, whereas the other was notable for a very mild scalp defect. Both appeared to have an unusual pulmonary lymphatic condition. The authors suggested a possible involvement of mesoderm in the morphogenesis of the disorder.

checks.evidence_quote: We report on two sibs with high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration (VRD), and occipital encephalocoele or scalp lesion.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.explanation: The authors suggest that mesoderm may be involved in the morphogenesis of the disorder. This comes up in their discussion of Knobloch syndrome and the reported sibs.

paragraphs.text: Antonarakis et al. (2021) studied a historical pedigree, published in 1998, with 2 affected sibs and normal parents; the phenotype was designated KNO2, Knobloch type 2 syndrome with intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, and encephalocele.

checks.evidence_quote: We studied an historical pedigree (published in 1998) designated as KNO2
checks.explanation: The abstract also states 'Whole exome sequencing of the two affected siblings and the normal parents', which covers the 2 sibs and normal parents.

checks.claim: Antonarakis et al. (2021) designated the phenotype in the 1998 pedigree KNO2, Knobloch type 2 syndrome with intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, and encephalocele.
checks.evidence_quote: designated as KNO2 (Knobloch type 2 syndrome with intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, encephalocele)
checks.explanation: The designation and its full description match the claim.

paragraphs.text: Antonarakis et al. (2021) concluded that KNO2 in the family they studied was dominant. The causative PAK2 variant was monoallelic and apparently de novo in both affected sibs, indicating likely germline mosaicism in one of the parents, although mosaicism could not be detected by deep sequencing of parental blood DNA.

checks.evidence_quote: The variant was monoallelic and apparently de novo in both siblings

checks.claim: Mosaicism for the PAK2 variant could not be detected by deep sequencing of parental blood DNA in the KNO2 family.
checks.evidence_quote: the mosaicism, however, could not be observed after deep sequencing of blood parental DNA
checks.explanation: Deep sequencing of parental blood DNA did not show the mosaicism.

paragraphs.text: In a family from New Zealand with Knobloch syndrome, Menzel et al. (2004) excluded linkage to the COL18A1 locus on chromosome 21q22.3, providing evidence for a second Knobloch syndrome locus. Mutation analysis also excluded COL15A1 as the gene responsible for KNO2.

checks.claim: In a family from New Zealand with Knobloch syndrome, Menzel et al. (2004) excluded linkage to the COL18A1 locus on chromosome 21q22.3.
checks.evidence_quote: Linkage to the COL18A1 locus was excluded in the New Zealand family
checks.explanation: The abstract also gives COL18A1's location as 21q22.3.

checks.claim: Exclusion of linkage to COL18A1 in the New Zealand Knobloch syndrome family provided evidence for a second Knobloch syndrome locus.
checks.evidence_quote: Linkage to the COL18A1 locus was excluded in the New Zealand family, providing evidence for the existence of a second KNO locus.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Mutation analysis by Menzel et al. (2004) excluded COL15A1 as the gene responsible for KNO2.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation analysis excluded COL15A1, a member of the multiplexin collagen subfamily similar to COL18A1, as being responsible for KNO2.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: Menzel et al. (2004) analyzed 2 unrelated Knobloch syndrome families, from Hungary and New Zealand. Two COL18A1 mutations were identified in the Hungarian family, whereas linkage to COL18A1 was excluded in the New Zealand family, demonstrating genetic heterogeneity.

checks.evidence_quote: Analysis of two unrelated KNO families from Hungary and New Zealand
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Two COL18A1 mutations were identified in the Hungarian Knobloch syndrome family studied by Menzel et al. (2004).
checks.evidence_quote: Two COL18A1 mutations were identified in the Hungarian family
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Linkage to COL18A1 was excluded in the New Zealand Knobloch syndrome family studied by Menzel et al. (2004).
checks.evidence_quote: Linkage to the COL18A1 locus was excluded in the New Zealand family
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: The findings of Menzel et al. (2004) demonstrated genetic heterogeneity in Knobloch syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: allowed us to confirm the involvement of COL18A1 in the pathogenesis of KNO and to demonstrate the existence of genetic heterogeneity.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: By whole-exome sequencing of the 2 affected sibs and their unaffected parents from a pedigree with KNO2, Antonarakis et al. (2021) identified a heterozygous (monoallelic) glu435-to-lys (E435K) substitution in the PAK2 gene as the causative variant. The variant was apparently de novo in both sibs, suggesting parental germline mosaicism, which was not detected by deep sequencing of parental blood DNA. The variant lies in the kinase domain, and structural analysis predicted possible compromise of kinase activity. In transfected HEK293T cells, the E435K variant resulted in partial loss of kinase activity.

checks.evidence_quote: Whole exome sequencing of the two affected siblings and the normal parents
checks.explanation: The abstract describes whole-exome sequencing of both affected siblings and both parents.

checks.claim: Antonarakis et al. (2021) identified a heterozygous (monoallelic) glu435-to-lys (E435K) substitution in the PAK2 gene as the causative variant in the 2 sibs with KNO2.
checks.evidence_quote: resulted in the identification of a PAK2 non-synonymous substitution p.(Glu435Lys) as a causative variant. The variant was monoallelic
checks.explanation: p.(Glu435Lys) is the same variant as E435K, and monoallelic means heterozygous.

checks.evidence_quote: The variant was monoallelic and apparently de novo in both siblings
checks.explanation: The variant is described as apparently de novo in both siblings.

checks.explanation: Deep sequencing of parental blood DNA did not show the mosaicism.

checks.explanation: The abstract places the variant in the kinase domain.

checks.evidence_quote: Structural analysis of the PAK2 p.(Glu435Lys) variant that is located in the kinase domain of the protein predicts a possible compromise in the kinase activity.
checks.explanation: The structural analysis predicts possible loss of kinase activity, as claimed.

checks.claim: In transfected HEK293T cells, the PAK2 E435K variant resulted in partial loss of kinase activity.
checks.evidence_quote: Functional analysis of the p.(Glu435Lys) PAK2 variant in transfected HEK293T cells results in a partial loss of the kinase activity.
checks.explanation: The functional result in HEK293T cells matches the claim.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) from a historical pedigree published in 1998, Antonarakis et al. (2021) identified a heterozygous glu435-to-lys (E435K) substitution in the kinase domain of the PAK2 gene, found by whole-exome sequencing of the sibs and their unaffected parents. The variant was apparently de novo in both sibs, suggesting parental germline mosaicism that was not detected by deep sequencing of parental blood DNA. In transfected HEK293T cells, the variant caused partial loss of kinase activity.

agent.process_note: All three papers are available only as abstracts; I read each in full. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the intro omits the PAK2 MIM number and chromosomal location. The Antonarakis et al. (2021) abstract refers to a 'historical pedigree (published in 1998)' but does not name Wilson et al. (1998) or the New Zealand family of Menzel et al. (2004), so I did not explicitly equate these families. The nucleotide change for PAK2 E435K is not given in the abstract.
